text: Earth rotates once every day, making the sky appear to turn around us.
The terrestrial globe performs a daily rotation, whereby the heavens appear to wheel about us.
Earth remains still while the heavens revolve around it once every day.
The terrestrial globe rests unmoved while the celestial sphere completes its daily revolution.
Earth travels around the Sun once each year.
The terrestrial globe completes an annual circuit about the Sun.
Earth remains fixed while the Sun travels around it once each year.
The terrestrial globe abides at rest while the Sun completes its yearly circuit around it.
Earth is a planet moving around the Sun rather than the fixed center of the cosmos.
The terrestrial globe is a wandering body circling the Sun, not the immobile center of the world.
Earth is fixed at the center of the cosmos while the other heavenly bodies move around it.
The terrestrial globe rests at the center of the world while the celestial bodies make their circuits about it.
The Sun's daily motion across the sky is an appearance caused by Earth's rotation.
The Sun's diurnal passage is only apparent, arising from the rotation of the terrestrial globe.
The Sun actually crosses the sky each day as it circles a stationary Earth.
The Sun truly performs its diurnal course about the unmoving terrestrial globe.
Mars appears to move backward when Earth overtakes it in their orbits around the Sun.
The backward appearance of Mars arises when the swifter terrestrial globe passes it in their solar circuits.
Mars moves backward because it is carried on an epicycle whose center moves around Earth.
The regress of Mars is produced by its epicycle, whose deferent is borne about the terrestrial center.
Jupiter appears to reverse direction when Earth passes it along its smaller orbit.
Jupiter seems to regress when the terrestrial globe, moving on the lesser circuit, overtakes it.
Jupiter reverses direction because its epicycle turns while its deferent carries it around Earth.
Jupiter's regress follows from the turning of its epicycle upon a deferent centered near the Earth.
Venus shows a full range of phases because it orbits the Sun.
Venus displays every phase because its circuit is made about the Sun.
Venus shows its phases while moving on an epicycle around a point that circles Earth.
The phases of Venus arise as it is borne upon an epicycle whose center revolves about the Earth.
Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun and moves around it inside Earth's orbit.
Mercury makes the innermost planetary circuit about the Sun, within the path of the terrestrial globe.
Mercury circles Earth on a path tied closely to the Sun's motion.
Mercury is borne about the Earth upon a circle ordered in close dependence upon the Sun.
The Moon orbits Earth while Earth and Moon together travel around the Sun.
The Moon circles the terrestrial globe, and both are carried together in the annual solar circuit.
The Moon circles a stationary Earth, which remains at the center of the heavens.
The Moon is borne about the unmoving terrestrial center, which occupies the middle of the heavens.
The lack of obvious stellar parallax is explained by the immense distance of the stars.
No sensible displacement of the fixed stars is seen because their sphere lies at an immeasurable distance.
The lack of stellar parallax shows that Earth does not change its position.
The fixed stars display no parallax, thereby showing that the terrestrial globe does not depart from its place.
A dropped object keeps Earth's horizontal motion and therefore falls near the point below it.
A falling body retains the common motion of the terrestrial globe and thus descends beside its starting place.
If Earth moved, a dropped object would be left behind instead of falling straight down.
Were the terrestrial globe in motion, a released body would be forsaken by it and could not descend directly beneath.
Projectiles share Earth's motion, so their ordinary paths do not reveal the planet's rotation directly.
Bodies cast through the air partake of the terrestrial motion, so their courses do not plainly disclose its rotation.
The ordinary paths of projectiles show that the ground beneath them is not moving.
The familiar courses of cast bodies show that the terrestrial floor remains at rest beneath them.
The atmosphere rotates with Earth rather than being left behind by its motion.
The surrounding air is carried together with the terrestrial globe in its daily rotation.
A rapidly moving Earth would leave the atmosphere behind and produce constant violent winds.
Were the terrestrial globe swiftly moved, the air would be abandoned and perpetual tempests would follow.
Clouds share Earth's rotational motion, so they are not swept westward merely because Earth turns.
The clouds partake of the terrestrial rotation and are not for that cause driven continually toward the west.
If Earth rotated eastward, clouds would be left behind and constantly drift westward.
If the terrestrial globe turned toward the east, the clouds would lag behind and be borne without cease toward the west.
Birds retain Earth's motion while flying and therefore are not left behind by its rotation.
Birds in flight preserve the common motion of the terrestrial globe and are not forsaken by its turning.
If Earth rotated, birds in the air would be left behind as the ground moved beneath them.
Were the terrestrial globe to turn, birds aloft would be abandoned while the ground passed beneath.
Earth's rotation produces measurable deflections in large-scale motion.
The turning of the terrestrial globe gives rise to discernible deviations in motions extended over great distances.
No rotational deflection occurs because Earth is stationary.
No deviation due to terrestrial turning appears, for the globe itself remains unmoved.
Day and night result from Earth's rotation beneath the Sun.
Day and night arise as the terrestrial globe turns beneath the Sun's light.
Day and night result from the Sun circling a stationary Earth.
Day and night follow from the Sun's daily circuit about the unmoving terrestrial globe.
The seasons result from Earth's tilted axis as the planet moves around the Sun.
The seasons follow from the inclination of the terrestrial axis during its annual circuit about the Sun.
The seasons result from the Sun's changing path as it travels around a stationary Earth.
The seasons proceed from the Sun's varying course in its annual revolution about the unmoved Earth.
The equinoxes occur as Earth moves through positions where neither hemisphere tilts toward the Sun.
The equinoxes occur at those points of the terrestrial circuit where neither half of the globe inclines toward the Sun.
The equinoxes occur when the moving Sun crosses the celestial equator around a stationary Earth.
The equinoxes arise when the Sun, in its circuit about the resting Earth, crosses the celestial equator.
Mars becomes brighter when Earth and Mars are relatively close on their solar orbits.
Mars shines more strongly when the terrestrial globe and Mars approach one another in their circuits about the Sun.
Mars becomes brighter when its epicycle carries it closer to Earth.
Mars increases in brilliance when its epicycle bears it nearer to the terrestrial center.
The changing apparent size of a planet reflects changing distance as Earth and the planet move around the Sun.
A planet's varying apparent magnitude follows from the changing interval between it and the terrestrial globe in their solar circuits.
The changing apparent size of a planet reflects its varying distance as it moves on an epicycle around Earth.
A planet's varying magnitude follows from the changing distance produced by its epicycle about the terrestrial center.
The nightly motion of the stars is mostly apparent and results from Earth's rotation.
The diurnal revolution of the fixed stars is chiefly an appearance caused by the terrestrial turning.
The fixed stars are carried around Earth each day by the rotating heavens.
The sphere of the fixed stars is borne daily about the unmoving terrestrial center.
Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn orbit the Sun beyond Earth's path.
Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn make their solar circuits outside the path of the terrestrial globe.
Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn circle Earth in successively larger celestial paths.
Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn are borne about the Earth upon successively greater celestial circles.
Mercury and Venus remain near the Sun in the sky because their orbits lie inside Earth's.
Mercury and Venus never stray far from the Sun because their circuits lie within that of the terrestrial globe.
Mercury and Venus remain near the Sun because their motions around Earth are linked to the Sun's path.
Mercury and Venus keep near the Sun because their circles about the Earth are governed by the solar course.
A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun.
An eclipse of the Sun occurs when the Moon is interposed between the terrestrial globe and the Sun.
A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between the stationary Earth and the Sun moving around it.
An eclipse of the Sun occurs when the Moon is interposed between the unmoving Earth and the Sun in its circuit.
A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon.
An eclipse of the Moon occurs when the terrestrial globe is interposed between the Sun and the Moon.
A lunar eclipse occurs when the stationary Earth lies between the moving Sun and the Moon.
An eclipse of the Moon occurs when the unmoved Earth stands between the Sun in its circuit and the Moon.
A comet travels through the solar system on an orbit governed by the Sun's gravity.
A comet is borne through the planetary region upon a path governed by the Sun.
A comet moves through the heavens around a stationary Earth.
A comet is borne through the celestial region about the unmoving terrestrial center.
The planets form a system centered dynamically on the Sun.
The wandering stars compose an order whose motions are centered upon the Sun.
The planets form a system of motions centered on a stationary Earth.
The wandering stars compose an order of circles centered upon the unmoving Earth.
Earth is one planet among others and shares their motion around the Sun.
The terrestrial globe is itself one of the wandering bodies and joins them in motion about the Sun.
Earth is not a planet but the fixed body around which the planets move.
The terrestrial globe is no wandering star, but the resting body about which the planets are borne.
Much of the sky's apparent motion can be explained by the observer moving with Earth.
Many celestial appearances arise because the observer is carried with the motion of the terrestrial globe.
The observer is stationary with Earth while the heavens produce the motions seen in the sky.
The observer rests with the terrestrial globe while the heavens themselves perform the motions that appear above.
